asDecan.p: Every sign is cut into three ten-degree slices, called decans, and each slice has its own planet and its own small card. Your Sun sits somewhere between 20 and 29 degrees of Capricorn, the last third of the sign, and in the Chaldean order that slice goes to the Sun itself. The Sun has no special dignity in Capricorn. It's a visitor there, neither helped nor held back, so it takes on the colour of Saturn, who rules the sign. What you get is Capricorn's patience and caution with the Sun's wish to be somebody sitting right in the middle of it. The Two of Pentacles, Jupiter's slice, is the juggler at the start of the sign. The Three, which belongs to Mars, is the craftsman on the job. By the time you get to yours the work is mostly done, and the question is what you keep. Have a look at the man in the picture with one coin held to his chest and two under his feet. The Devil is your Sun card, and this is the finer grain inside it.

You know roughly what's in your bank account at any given moment, and you'd be a bit embarrassed to say how often you check. At a restaurant with friends, when someone suggests splitting the bill evenly, you do a quick sum in your head about who had the wine, and mostly you say nothing. A Sunday with nothing planned tends to turn into a Sunday sorting something out, the spare room, the tax folder, the spreadsheet for the house. You lend your good tools reluctantly and you notice when they come back late. None of this is meanness, and the people who know you well can see that. The Sun here wants to be proud of something solid, and Saturn has taught it that solid things get lost when nobody's keeping an eye on them. So you keep an eye on them.

The gift people don't expect is that you're a very good keeper of other people's things. The family photos end up at your place. You're the one asked to be treasurer of the tennis club, to hold the spare key, to be named as executor, and it's because everyone can tell that what goes into your hands comes back out in better shape. When your grandmother's recipe book was falling apart, you were the one who had it rebound. The Sun likes being trusted with something that matters, and Saturn makes sure you don't drop it. There's a second part to it. You're usually right about what things are worth. Haggling over a second-hand car or a pay rise, you know the fair number, you hold it calmly, and people respect you for it far more than they'd say.

The shadow that's harder to spot is that you hold on to positions as well as possessions. Once you've put years into something, a job, a house, a way of doing the accounts at work, walking away feels like admitting the years were wasted, so you stay. I see this a lot with late Capricorn Suns. The house that's been too big since the kids left, kept because you paid it off. The role that stopped growing five years ago. There's pride tangled up in it, because the Sun in these degrees has built its sense of itself on what it's gathered, and letting any of it go feels like shrinking. It turns up in small ways too. You'll keep an argument from a family Christmas on file for years and bring it out exactly when it helps your case.

When something goes wrong, a job cut, a break-up, a big bill nobody saw coming, your first move is to batten down. You cancel the subscriptions, stop going out, go through the accounts line by line and tell everyone you're fine. That part is often useful, to be honest. About a week later the battening has spread. You've stopped answering messages, you're working late for no clear reason, and you've gone quiet at home in a way that's hard to live next to. Your partner or your kids can feel the lid on, and they tend to take it personally. What helps is letting one person see the actual numbers, the real size of the problem, whatever it is. Saturn tells you that you have to carry it alone. Once someone else has seen it, you usually loosen up enough to sleep.

The Devil is your Sun card, so attachment runs deep in you, and this slice turns it into keeping. You show love by providing, and by holding on to small things, the ticket from a first date still in a drawer twenty years later. What's less obvious is how awkward you are on the receiving end. An expensive present from someone new makes you uneasy, as if you now owe them, and you'll quietly work out how to even it up. Being looked after when you're sick is almost worse. It takes a long while before you hand anyone a key to your place, literal or otherwise. The partners who suit you are patient, reasonably settled in their own finances, and happy to let you run the household money for a year or two before they ask to see the books.

You're built for work where something has to be looked after over a long stretch. Finance, property, running a family business, managing a museum collection or a pension fund, the operations side of any place that can't afford to lose things. The Three of Pentacles people next door love the craft of the job itself. You care about what the job adds up to over ten years, and the Sun in you wants a title you've earned and a desk that's properly yours. Where it goes wrong is handing things over. You'll keep doing the budget yourself long after you've got a team, because giving it away means trusting someone else with what you've guarded, and you end up with a team that never learns how. Each year, pick one piece of your job and give it away properly.

At twenty this decan can seem old for its age. Saving hard, living carefully, a bit judgemental about friends who spend their wages on a trip to Bali. There's often a family story behind it, a lean patch or a parent who worried about money out loud. By the mid-thirties most people with a Sun here have built something real, a deposit, a position, some standing, and the job becomes deciding how much of it needs guarding. That's usually when the first hard lesson about holding too tight arrives, a friendship or a relationship that went cold from it. These degrees sit at the end of Capricorn, already leaning toward Aquarius, and the fifties often bring that side out. People start giving on purpose, helping the grandchildren with a deposit, backing a cause they care about, and they seem lighter for it.

Once a month, give away something you'd normally keep. It doesn't have to be money. A book you'll never reread, handed to someone who'd like it. An afternoon of your weekend helping a friend move house. The good bottle you were saving for an occasion, opened on an ordinary Wednesday with whoever's around. Write one line about what you gave and how it felt the next day. After six months, read the list back to yourself.
